funding: Owned and run by the City of Bordeaux with support from DRAC Nouvelle-Aquitaine (French state). 2023 patrons named by the museum: Les Amis du Capc, Cultura, Banque Palatine and CIC (major patrons), plus Lacoste, Unikalo, Château Haut-Selve, Château de Camensac and Hôtel de Normandie.
why_flagged: In 2018 the City of Bordeaux dismissed director María Inés Rodríguez, and 79 art-world figures publicly criticised municipal pressure and shrinking funds.
other_findings: In March 2018 the City of Bordeaux dismissed director María Inés Rodríguez citing 'managerial difficulties' (The Art Newspaper, Hyperallergic).
City culture deputy Fabien Robert asked 'Does contemporary art still exist?' and proposed the CAPC become a 'vitrine' (Hyperallergic).
79 artists and curators signed an open letter in Libération criticising recurring municipal pressure and shrinking funds at the museum and asking the culture minister to investigate (Hyperallergic).
bottom_line: The CAPC is a city-owned museum funded mainly by the City of Bordeaux with state support through the DRAC, plus banks, retailers and Bordeaux wine estates as patrons. No funding problem was found; the record's €3.8M budget figure could not be confirmed. Worth watching: the 2018 political dismissal of its director over the city's direction for the museum.

funding: Run by the state-owned Vorarlberger Kulturhäuser-Betriebsgesellschaft and subsidised by the State of Vorarlberg (€2.0M in 2011, projected €2.6M by 2014 per the state audit office). Principal sponsor Hypo Vorarlberg; also vkw, Zumtobel, KUB Freunde, Mader Flatz Schett, UNIQA (2026) and Hugo Boss (prize).
why_flagged: Principal sponsor Hypo Vorarlberg was named in the 2016 Panama Papers, and sponsor illwerke vkw also sells natural gas.
other_findings: In April 2016 Hypo Vorarlberg CEO Michael Grahammer resigned after the bank was named in the Panama Papers; he denied the bank broke any laws (AFP via ARY News).

Austria's financial market authority reviewed Hypo Vorarlberg's accounts in 2016; a 2012 probe into a Virgin Islands firm linked to US-sanctioned Gennady Timchenko was dropped in 2013 for lack of evidence (AFP via ARY News).
illwerke vkw, mainly owned by the State of Vorarlberg, runs hydropower but also supplies natural gas and operates the regional gas grid (company presentation 2025).
The state audit office reported in 2012 that KUB's subsidy would rise from €2.0M to €2.6M by 2014 because a main sponsor dropped out (vol.at).
bottom_line: KUB is a state institution funded mainly by the State of Vorarlberg, with sponsors that are largely state-owned regional companies. Nothing found against the museum itself; worth watching are the principal sponsor's 2016 Panama Papers exposure and vkw's gas business.

funding: Owned and run by the Kunstverein in Bremen (about 10,000 members); public funding from the City of Bremen (€2.7M a year budgeted in 2016/17) covers roughly 40% of the budget, with the rest from members, foundations and sponsors.
why_flagged: A funder, the Hermann Reemtsma Stiftung, is cigarette-family money, and the museum has faced Nazi-era restitution claims in 2024 and 2025.
other_findings: The Hermann Reemtsma Stiftung was founded in 1988 by Hermann-Hinrich Reemtsma and is named for his father, cigarette maker Hermann F. Reemtsma; it distributes €4–6M a year (reflecta).
In October 2024 the German Advisory Commission rejected the George Grosz heirs' claim to two paintings, finding the loss stemmed from debts to Alfred Flechtheim predating 1933 (ARTnews, Volksstimme).
In April 2025 the Kunsthalle kept Pissarro's 'Girl Lying in the Grass', sold in 1942 by Jaap van den Bergh while in hiding, after a compensation agreement with his heir (Jüdische Allgemeine).
The museum has returned several Nazi-looted works between 2009 and 2016 and provenance research on Bremen dealers continues (Wikipedia).
funders: Senator für Kultur, Freie Hansestadt Bremen
bottom_line: The Kunsthalle is a privately owned association museum with substantial Bremen state subsidy and foundation support. Nothing found against its own finances; worth watching are tobacco-family foundation money and the handling of Nazi-era provenance claims.
